title: Multiorbital driving of quantum geometric nonlinear transport in oxide interfaces
summary: Quantum geometry plays a relevant role in determining the intrinsic non-linear transport properties of low-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the quantum geometric contribution to the non-linear conductivity in $\text{SrTiO}_3$-based two-dimensional electron gases, comparing the prototypical (001) and (111) crystallographic interface orientations. Using a multi-orbital tight-binding approach, we uncover the crucial role of the multiband electronic structure in determining the quantum-geometric contribution to nonlinear transport. In particular, we show how the hybridization of $t_{2g}$ orbitals near avoided band crossings shapes the momentum-space distribution of the band-normalized quantum metric and the resulting nonlinear conductivity. Furthermore, we reveal a strong dependence on crystal orientation: while the (001) interface exhibits sharp peak-and-dip features confined around Lifshitz transitions, the trigonal symmetry of the (111) interface promotes strong orbital mixing. Our results highlight how the interplay between orbital hybridization and crystallographic orientation gives rise to distinct quantum-geometric nonlinear transport responses in oxide interfaces.

title: Wireless readout and control of cavity magnon-polaritons via photonic modes delocalised across a gap
summary: In cavity magnonics, photon-magnon hybridisation is typically detected by measuring the cavity response (i.e. measuring cavity resonance shifts through its reflection or transmission spectra). While a large body of work in the field has focused on three-dimensional cavities, a variety of two-dimensional resonators have also been explored as hosts for photonic modes due to their compatibility with on-chip integration. Nevertheless, the readout approach remains largely unchanged. Here, we demonstrate remote excitation and readout of cavity magnon-polaritons using two spatially separated, wirelessly coupled ring resonators. Through inductive coupling, energy is transferred between the resonators, enabling the magnonic system to be excited by one resonator while its hybrid-mode spectrum is detected through measurements of the other. We demonstrate wireless readout of cavity magnon-polaritons at separations ranging from millimetres to centimetres, identifying their characteristic response in the remotely measured spectrum. This establishes wireless resonator coupling as a route to remote interrogation of hybrid photon-magnon systems.

title: Spherical HgTe nanocrystal: a multi-band effective mass study
summary: The size-quantized energies, eigenstates, and optical selection rules in a spherical HgTe nanocrystal are studied by solving the multi-band effective-mass equations analytically. The six-band Kane model, involving both the $Γ_{6}$ and $Γ_{8}$ bands within the spherical approximation, is employed in the derivation. The eigenstates can be classified by both the total angular momentum and the parity. As the nanocrystal radius varies, crossings occur not only between electron and hole energy levels but also among the hole levels themselves. The lowest two electron states (in each spin subspace) are surface states, one with even parity and the other with odd parity. The optical selection rules consist of two parts, namely, the parity selection and the angular momentum selection.

title: Quantum Hall Effect in a 3D Cross-Dimensional Quantum Anomalous Hall System
summary: We systematically investigate cross-dimensional transport and the resulting quantum Hall effect in 3D quantum anomalous Hall effect systems, which are constructed by coupling two Weyl-semimetal Hamiltonians. Our study unveils that the system hosts highly anisotropic surface states and chiral modes, leading to rich quantum Hall responses. Crucially, we clarify how magnetic fields applied along three high-symmetry directions dictate the evolution of the Chern numbers, chiral modes, and Hall responses. We discover that chiral modes along different directions can originate from distinct mechanisms, giving rise to various magnetic modulation characteristics. Furthermore, we unveil the breakdown of the conventional Chern-number-based bulk-boundary correspondence under magnetic fields, where the Chern numbers alone fail to fully characterize the evolution of the chiral states. This anomalous behavior is attributed to the unique momentum-space distributions of surface bands. These insights are further validated numerically through multi-terminal Hall transport simulations. Our findings expand the understanding of magnetic-field-driven mechanisms in 3D topological systems and provide deeper insights into the interplay between quantized Hall effects and Chern numbers in 3D systems.

title: Oscillatory superconducting proximity effects in a buried Pt interlayer detected by FMR
summary: We investigate superconducting proximity effects in NbN/Pt/Py and NbN/Cu/Py trilayers using broadband ferromagnetic resonance (FMR). The reduction of the spin-pumping contribution to the Py damping below the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is used to probe the superconducting correlations and electronic density of state in the buried metallic interlayer. For a Cu interlayer, the damping reduction remains finite up to at least 20 nm, in agreement with the large coherence length above 100nm in Cu. In contrast, the damping reduction for a Pt interlayer exhibits a non-monotonic thickness dependence and is fully suppressed above 5 nm. Using the quasiclassical theory, we are able to explain the oscillation in damping reduction below Tc with the coexistence of superconducting and magnetic proximity effects in Pt, which generates oscillations of the superconducting order parameter and electronic density of state in the exchange-splitted Pt interlayer. Our results establish spin-pumping damping as a sensitive probe of superconducting proximity effects in buried metallic layers.

title: Local Pressure Induced Quantum Dot to Ring Transition and Aharonov Bohm Effect in Reconfigurable MoTe2 Bilayers
summary: We demonstrate that local pressure provides an effective means of engineering reconfigurable quantum confinement in MoTe2 homobilayers. By applying a smooth, spatially varying pressure profile, we show that the confinement geometry can be continuously tuned from a conventional quantum dot to a quantum ring, with the emergence of annular confinement being a distinctive feature of AB-stacked bilayers. This crossover originates from the pressure-induced spatial modulation in the electronic parameters, which produces an off-center minimum in the effective confinement potential, thereby redistributing the ground-state probability density away from the center and giving rise to an annular confinement geometry. In the quantum-ring regime, a perpendicular magnetic field gives rise to a flux-periodic energy spectrum and persistent currents, providing characteristic signatures of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. By coupling the pressure-induced quantum ring to source and drain leads, we further demonstrate pronounced Aharonov-Bohm conductance oscillations, accompanied by real-space current patterns exhibiting constructive and destructive interference at integer and half-integer magnetic flux quanta, respectively. These findings establish locally pressurized MoTe2 bilayers as a lithography-free platform for reconfigurable quantum confinement and realizing pressure-tunable Aharonov-Bohm interferometry in two dimensional materials.

title: Curling Superconducting Vortices by Nematic Fluxon-Skyrmion Interaction
summary: Superconducting vortex represents a topological entity in type-II superconductors, where the prototypical manifestation of such a macroscopic quantum state holds great promise for applications in future quantum technologies. Deterministic control of the vortex dynamics at the nanoscale is central to enhance superconductors' critical thresholds and design next-generation superconducting quantum devices. However, it is still scientifically challenging due to the intrinsic nature of the vortex pinning landscapes in superconductors. Here, we observe an even-in-field Hall-like signal with about two order of magnitude enhancement in a type-II superconductor/chiral magnet heterostructure, which confines to the field-temperature window where the flux flow coexists with magnetic skyrmions. The polarity of such a giant even-in-field transverse response reverses between orthogonal current directions, suggesting an on-track vortex flow driven by a nematic fluxon-skyrmion interaction analyzed via the extended vortex-viscosity tensor. More critically, a deterministic manipulation of skyrmions at the nanoscale within the hybrid system enables selective and reversible controls over the dissipative behavior and therefore the reconfigurable fluxon transport, mimic the precise control of curling stone in winter Olympic, thereby opening a new avenue towards the exploration of programmable topological and superconducting quantum devices.

title: Floquet-Induced Valley Polarization and Topological Phases in Twisted Bilayer Graphene Heterostructures
summary: We theoretically investigate twisted bilayer graphene (tTBG) heterostructures subjected to circularly polarized light. Inversion symmetry is broken through the combined application of an out-of-plane electric field and the incorporation of insulating substrates, enabling precise control of the valley degrees of freedom and associated topological phases. We identify a regime in which the valley degeneracy is lifted: one valley retains a gapless, linear Dirac-like dispersion, whereas the other develops a finite band gap and becomes electronically inactive. The interplay between Floquet driving and inversion-symmetry breaking induces topological phase transitions characterized by Chern numbers C = -2, C = -1, and C = 0, together with the emergence of perfectly valley-polarized domain-wall channels. Furthermore, magnetic asymmetry arising from proximity to adjacent two-dimensional ferromagnetic contacts enables spin-valley filtering. These findings establish the potential of graphene-based heterostructures as highly tunable systems for controlling spin and valley degrees of freedom.

title: A High-Frequency Flux-Driven DC-SQUID Threshold Detector at the Single-Microwave-Photon Energy Scale: A Numerical Feasibility Study
summary: In our recent work (Phys. Rev. B \textbf{113}, 224503 (2026)), we showed numerically that rapidly sweeping the bias current of a current-biased Josephson junction threshold detector (CBJJ-JTD) drives it out of equilibrium. This substantially reduces the effect of thermal noise on microwave detection and may enable threshold detection near the energy of a single microwave photon. The scheme requires very low damping ($β\leq 10^{-4}$) and a very fast bias-current sweep ($v/β\geq 1$), both of which are difficult to achieve with available junctions and low-pass-filtered cryogenic measurement lines. Here we propose a more experimentally accessible nonequilibrium threshold detector based on a high-frequency flux-driven direct-current superconducting quantum interference device (DC-SQUID) and investigate it by numerically solving the resistively and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) equations. The applied flux drives a circulating supercurrent and sustains nonequilibrium phase dynamics throughout the bias-current sweep, removing the need for a fast sweep or for transient oscillations set by the initial phase. Using typical experimental device parameters, we calculate switching-current distributions (SCDs) with and without a microwave input for both driven and undriven SQUIDs. We quantify detection performance using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and their area under the curve (AUC). The simulations show that high-frequency flux drive reduces the impact of thermal noise and enables statistical discrimination of weak microwave pulses at the single-photon energy scale. We also numerically estimate detector characteristics such as phase selectivity and dynamic range.

title: Interface invariants of rhombohedral graphene with layer-dependent potentials and couplings
summary: Domain walls in the perpendicular bias of rhombohedral (ABC-stacked) graphene bind valley-resolved interface modes whose signed number is fixed by a bulk-difference invariant. We determine which values of this invariant are reachable when the layer potentials are arbitrary monotone profiles, as produced by screening, and when the interlayer couplings vary from bond to bond. Within the single-particle continuum model, the invariant of an $m$-layer stack equals the difference of occupied angular weights of the zero-momentum levels, which reduces the classification to the ordering of those levels. At equal coupling, nonlinear monotone potentials reproduce exactly the set of invariants of linear potentials, also under the requirement of a common energy gap: screening moves phase boundaries but creates no new invariant values. With bond-dependent coupling, we characterize all occupied configurations. The range of attainable invariants is unchanged, but the gaps inside it are filled, beginning at five layers. Reflection-symmetric stacks realize a large subfamily with a guaranteed common gap, and lower bounds on single-bulk gaps complete the set of invariants with a common global gap for five and six layers. Among the examples is an eight-layer domain wall defined purely by gates, whose number of co-propagating channels per valley switches from 8 to 16 as the gate strength increases. Exact transfer-matrix calculations of the interface spectrum reproduce every predicted signed crossing count. A norm bound gives the minimum spread of interlayer coupling compatible with a prescribed gap.

title: Minimal Three-Band Model and $d$-Wave Superconductivity in La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_8$
summary: Motivated by the recent observation of ambient-pressure superconductivity in Pr- and Y-substituted La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_8$, we combined density-functional theory (DFT), dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), random phase approximation (RPA), and fluctuation exchange approximation (FLEX) methods to study its electronic structure and superconducting pairing symmetry. DFT band analysis indicates that the low-energy states are mainly dominated by three Ni-3$d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals with weak $d$-$p$ hybridization. Multi-orbital DMFT calculations yield an average $d_{x^2-y^2}$ filling of about 0.87, close to the optimal value for infinite-layer nickelates. By comparing the DMFT results of $d_{x^2-y^2}$ only and full Ni-3$d$ models, we find that their electronic properties are almost completely consistent, demonstrating the effectiveness of the simplified $d_{x^2-y^2}$ model. RPA and FLEX calculations based on this model consistently indicate a dominant $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave pairing instability. These results establish La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_8$ as a system whose electronic structure closely resembles that of hole-doped cuprates, suggesting that the electronic pockets near the $Γ$- and $A$-points, which are characteristic of infinite-layer nickelates, may not be essential for superconductivity. The calculated superconducting transition temperature ($T_C$) is approximately 10\,K, in good agreement with experimental observations.

title: Population of spin orbit-split-electron branches in semimetallic HgTe quantum wells
summary: We present the results of experimental studies on magnetoresistance, the Hall effect, and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations performed in gated heterostructures with HgTe-based gapless semiconductor quantum wells. We show that in quantum wells with widths corresponding to a semimetallic charge carrier spectrum, electrons, in contrast to the idealized model, populate both spin-orbit-split branches of the spectrum. This occurs regardless of whether the Fermi level lies exclusively in the conduction band or within the conduction-valence band overlap region.

title: Thickness-Dependent Morphology and Electrical Transport in Ultrathin Amorphous MoSi Films
summary: We investigate the thickness-dependent surface morphology and electrical transport of ultrathin amorphous Mo50Si50 films deposited by magnetron co-sputtering. Atomic force microscopy of Si-capped heterostructures on Si/SiO2 reveals smooth surfaces throughout the investigated thickness range, with RMS roughness below 0.2 nm and a non-monotonic thickness dependence characterized by a minimum at 1.92 nm. Room-temperature sheet resistance follows an approximately inverse-thickness dependence for films with nominal thicknesses of about 1.9-5 nm, whereas a pronounced deviation from this scaling develops below approximately 1.5-2 nm. Temperature-dependent measurements further reveal a superconducting transition in the 30-nm film, while the 1.54-nm film shows a strong resistance increase upon cooling clearly indicates a superconductor-insulator transition. In the 2-20 K range, the sheet conductance of the 1.54-nm film exhibits a reproducible logarithmic temperature dependence, Gs(T)=G0+Bln(T/T0), consistent with quantum corrections to diffusive transport in a strongly disordered quasi-two-dimensional conductor. These results identify a thickness-sensitive transport regime in ultrathin MoSi while demonstrating that the corresponding heterostructures retain comparatively smooth surface morphology.

title: FlakeForge: automated lithography-ready device layout from optical images of exfoliated van der Waals flakes
summary: Fabricating a device from an exfoliated van der Waals flake requires finding a suitable flake under a microscope and designing its lithography layout by hand. We present FlakeForge, an open-source pipeline from raw optical images of a marker-patterned chip to a lithography-ready, multilayer design file. It scores flakes for device usability, aligns and scales each image from its markers, fits the user's device design to each selected flake's contour and connects every contact to a bond pad by a trace routed around all earlier devices, so no two overlap. Demonstrated on Hall bars and Little-Parks rings, it processed four chips in about half an hour, work that took an expert days. It runs fully unattended or pauses for user review. Adapting it to a new material, marker design or device dimensions requires only configuration, with no training data; a new device type requires only its geometry definition.

title: Charge-fluctuation hot lines and superconductivity in Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$BiO$_3$
summary: The origin of superconductivity near 30~K in Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$BiO$_3$ has remained a long-standing puzzle. Tunneling experiments give an electron--boson coupling $λ\approx 0.7$--1.2, whereas density-functional calculations give $λ\approx 0.3$, concentrated in the breathing mode near 50--70~meV. We propose that the missing coupling of about 0.7 comes from dynamical charge fluctuations at Q=(pi,pi,pi)/a, the ordering vector of the charge-disproportionated parent compound, and introduce an overdamped boson model to describe them. Using a tight-binding fit to the conduction band found from density-functional calculations at $x=0.4$, we show that such a boson scatters electrons strongly only on hot lines of the Fermi surface, small loops around the $\langle 111\rangle$ directions where k and k+Q are both at the Fermi level. We derive closed-form self-energies, quasiparticle residues and band reconstructions, including shadow bands and hot-line pseudogaps for long-range correlations, and show that a sum rule fixes the Fermi-surface-averaged coupling independently of the boson frequency and correlation length. Combining the LDA phonon with an overdamped mode of frequency $ω_m\approx 25$~meV and coupling $λ\approx 0.7$, anisotropic Eliashberg calculations reproduce $T_c\approx 25$--30~K for correlation lengths of two to three lattice spacings and predict a gap enhanced by a factor of 3--4 on the hot loops. For longer correlation lengths an $s$-wave state competes closely with a sign-changing $T_{2g}$ state confined to the hot loops. In the random-phase approximation for an extended Hubbard model, the boson emerges naturally near a charge instability at $R$, but purely electronic fluctuations are too weak and too long-ranged; coupling to the breathing-mode lattice distortion is one possible way to strengthen them.

title: Kinetic inductance of two-dimensional viscous electron fluid
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, to be published in JETP Letters
summary: Modern high-mobility two-dimensional electron systems are pure enough to manifest hydrodynamic regime of electron transport similar to dynamics of classical fluids. With the bulk scattering controlled by momentum-conserving electron-electron collisions, these novel hydrodynamic materials demonstrate systematic violation of conventional metallic behavior due to the Drude model in stationary electric transport. In this letter, we study the linear reactive AC response of 2D electron fluid in a narrow channel geometry and show that the essentially non-local viscous dissipation induces non-trivial size effect in it. In particular, kinetic inductance, which represents collective inertia of the entire electron fluid, is enhanced by non-uniform flow profile and, in contrast to diffusive transport, dominates the electrical impedance already in collisional regime by virtue of viscous skin effect. The onset of reactive behavior falls within the microwave frequency domain in the state-of-the-art 2D hydrodynamic conductors which makes them promising material system for applications in high-frequency electronics at elevated temperatures.

title: Tuning of superconducting and physical properties of Mo$_{1-x}$Si$_x$ thin films for Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detector Applications
summary: We investigate the normal-state electrical properties of ultrathin amorphous Mo$_{1-x}$Si$_x$ films deposited by DC magnetron co-sputtering over a broad range of compositions and thicknesses. Films with Si contents of $x = 0.14$ to $0.5$ were deposited on Si/SiO$_2$ and Si/Si$_3$N$_4$ substrates (monocrystalline Si with SiO$_2$ and S$_3$N$_4$ buffer layers respectfully); X-ray diffraction confirms an amorphous structure across the full composition range, while X-ray reflectometry is used to verify film thicknesses. The room-temperature sheet resistance ranges from 110 to 1990 $Ω/\square$, corresponding to resistivities of 125-478 $μΩ\cdot$cm. The sheet resistance generally increases with increasing Si content and decreasing film thickness, although the coupled variation of composition and thickness limits the quantitative separation of these effects. Additional measurements on thicker reference films show superconducting transition temperatures between 5.2 and 7.7 K, with $T_c$ decreasing monotonically at higher Si contents. A comparison of films on different substrate types shows no systematic difference between Si/SiO$_2$ and Si/Si$_3$N$_4$, while films on Al$_2$O$_3$ exhibit elevated sheet resistance at the lower thicknesses. These results characterize the accessible parameter space of our deposition process and provide a basis for the selection of film stoichiometry for detector fabrication.

title: Sondheimer oscillations in Weyl semimetal films
summary: In conducting films subject to an out-of-plane magnetic field, electron motion between the surfaces gives rise to conductance oscillations periodic in magnetic field, known as Sondheimer oscillations. While this size effect has been investigated in conventional metals, its dependence on the Berry curvature of topological materials remains less explored. In this work, we extend the semiclassical Boltzmann description of Sondheimer oscillations to type-I Weyl semimetal films. We account for the Berry curvature, the orbital magnetic moment and the effect of the Zeeman coupling on the Fermi wavevector and the electronic group velocity. The Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment generate a beating pattern and chirping in the Sondheimer oscillations. In the thick-film and thin-film regimes, we provide analytical expressions for the longitudinal conductivity, which highlight the interplay between electronic band topology and boundary-scattering in magnetotransport.

title: Auditing a superconducting database built by a large language model
summary: The data on superconducting materials are published as measurements and scattered across the literature, in prose, in tables and in figures, so that gathering them into one place means reading the papers themselves. Large language models (LLMs) can read those papers, and databases built that way are appearing. The difficulty is not the reading but the trust: a number lifted out of a sentence can belong to a neighbouring compound, a computed transition temperature can be recorded without saying that it is computed, and the paper itself may be wrong. This paper describes a pipeline that extracts superconducting materials from the published literature with an LLM, checks every value against its source, and asks how far that checking goes. The pipeline proposed 19,576 records; a cascade of gates rejected 659,252 field-level extractions, 644,438 of them for want of verbatim evidence, 13,121 because the text does not attach the value to the material, and 1,693 because the source sentence reads as a calculation. The database that survives holds 3,137 material records, each with the sentence its value came from. An audit of the survivors by two independent models, on 500 records drawn in proportion to the database, shows that the gates remove the errors that are mechanical: in 93.4% of the audited records the value is in the text and the text is about the compound the record names, and 91.8% of them are measurements rather than predictions.

title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
summary: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.

title: Mixed-State Magnetotransport Below $T_c$ in Type-II Superconducting NbN Thin Films
summary: The transport properties of type-II superconductors in the mixed state below the superconducting transition temperature, $T_c$, remain difficult to interpret because superconducting and dissipative processes coexist in the presence of a magnetic field. To investigate this regime in NbN thin films, we measured the field-dependent sheet resistance ($R^M_{xx}$) and Hall resistance ($R^M_{xy}$) below $T_c$ in Van der Pauw geometry for 4-nm-thick NbN films on sapphire and silicon substrates at driving currents of 1 mA and 2 mA. By combining the longitudinal response with the antisymmetrized Hall signal, we use a phenomenological current-partition model to estimate the dissipative and superconducting current contributions. From this analysis, we estimate the field-dependent superconducting current together with the Hall-derived effective dissipative carrier density and mobility. We also observe an even-in-field transverse signal whose magnitude depends strongly on the driving current. We discuss this signal as a possible mixed-state response involving the magnetic and supercurrent texture of Abrikosov vortices, vortex dynamics, and Cooper-pair current redistribution. The present measurements do not uniquely distinguish vortex, condensate, or combined contributions. The model provides a practical way to compare the longitudinal and transverse mixed-state responses without implying a direct spatial separation of the two current channels.

title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, including End Matter; Supplemental Material: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Code: https://github.com/caidish/KlayoutClaw
summary: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

title: Valence band, electron correlation, and possible temperature dependent change in the electronic structure near $E_F$ of a candidate of ambient-pressure nickelate superconductors Sr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$
summary: Photoemission spectroscopy (PES) studies of Sr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_5$Cl$_2$ (Sr3252), a candidate ambient-pressure bilayer nickelate superconductor, have been performed to investigate the electronic structure. Valence band spectra, which are compared with DFT and DFT+U calculations, reveal dominant Ni 3$d$ $t_{2g}$-derived states located around 0.6 eV binding energy with a shoulder around 0.2 eV that can be attributed to states with a dominant Ni 3$d_{3z2-r2}$ character. The overall valence band shape is better reproduced by the simulated spectrum of DFT+U (= 3 eV), providing an experimental estimation of the strength of electron correlation. High-resolution PES near the Fermi level ($E_F$) exhibits marked temperature dependence, which cannot be fully understood by a broadening due to coupling of a photo-hole to phonons alone and suggests change in electronic structure. The results provide fundamental electronic structure information of Sr3252, which is useful to further explore the superconductivity of Sr3252.

title: A Unified Energy-Density Framework for Moiré Interface Energetics and Mechanics
summary: The mechanical response of moiré interfaces depends on how atomic registry combines with contact size and boundary geometry. An analytical description must retain this discrete lattice information while connecting microscopic interactions to the energetics of finite contacts. Here, we develop a unified energy-density framework for rigid van der Waals interfaces by expressing registry-dependent pair potentials and atomic densities in reciprocal space. The resulting formulation accommodates different lattice bases and atomic species, linking single-atom and molecular adsorption to infinite bilayers and finite crystalline contacts. Explicit expressions for circular and regular polygonal flakes separate the area contribution from boundary-dependent terms and connect microscopic corrugation coefficients to energy barriers, rotational torques, and interlayer shear stiffnesses. The boundary analysis recovers the quarter-power area scaling of the barrier envelope for circular flakes and distinguishes bounded oscillations from square-root area scaling for polygonal contacts according to edge orientation. A dimensionless criterion characterizes the polygon-to-circle crossover in terms of moiré wavelength, flake size, and side number. Direct-summation benchmarks support the finite-domain expressions, while calculations for two-dimensional ice on graphene demonstrate the corresponding boundary-scaling trends in a molecular lattice. Applications to interlayer shear and graphite compression connect the same microscopic interaction description to tangential and normal mechanical responses. The framework establishes an analytical connection between microscopic registry, moiré periodicity, and finite-domain geometry, providing a basis for understanding and tailoring the energetics and mechanics of van der Waals contacts.

title: Soliton Propagation of Zero Sound in Superfluid $^3$He-B
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, includes correction to the typesetting error in Eq.7 of the published version
summary: Nonlinear equations for zero sound interacting with the B-phase collective modes are derived by treating $^3$He-B as a medium of two-level ``molecules'' (Cooper pairs), The nonlinear equations reduce to known results from kinetic theory in the linear response limit. Soliton solutions to the nonlinear equations are discussed in context with the experiments of Polturak et al.

title: Quantum Geometry Effects in Lattice Dynamics
summary: Quantum geometric effects such as the Berry curvature and the quantum metric are well established in electronic transport, whereas in lattice dynamics the Berry curvature also plays a key role: adiabatically following the lattice, electrons generate a molecular Berry curvature that splits degenerate optical phonons into chiral partners. To determine how the quantum metric affects phonons, we go beyond adiabatic lattice dynamics, identifying Berry curvature and quantum metric contributions to the electronic response of the lattice. Using first-principles calculations in the magnetic topological semimetal EuB$_6$, we find that phonon modes with chiral splitting and those with nonchiral splitting coexist. Unlike the former, which originate from the Berry curvature, the latter arise from the pure quantum metric, while the Berry curvature contribution is forbidden by crystal symmetry.

title: Spin-controlled thermophase and noise-optimized thermometry in multiorbital quantum dots
summary: Converting temperature differences into electrical signals underlies both thermoelectric energy conversion and thermometry, which is essential for managing heat in cryogenic quantum technologies. Superconducting circuits typically show a weak thermoelectric response, since their quasiparticle spectrum is nearly particle-hole symmetric. In a Josephson junction, a temperature difference can instead be converted into a superconducting phase difference in an open circuit. We investigate this thermophase effect in a setup where the junction consists of a two-orbital quantum dot with Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Zeeman splitting. A second orbital near the superconducting coherence peaks supports quasiparticle transport over a broad gate range. Zeeman splitting can enhance the thermophase by suppressing pair transport, while spin-orbit hybridization shifts the orbital resonances and can reverse the sign of the response. We assess the junction as a phase-based thermometer using a noise budget that includes readout and current noise together with fluctuations of the orbital energies and the magnetic field. The optimal operating points do not maximize the thermophase but balance a large quasiparticle response against sensitivity to parameter fluctuations. Under experimentally motivated noise assumptions, we obtain projected noise-equivalent temperatures of order $10\,μ\mathrm{K}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and determine the range over which a linear calibration remains accurate. Gate-tunable quantum-dot junctions thus offer a phase-based route to sensing temperature differences in superconducting circuits at sub-kelvin temperatures.

title: Anatomy of orbital and spin responses in GaAs and Si: Hall, inverse Faraday, and magneto-optical Kerr effects
summary: Magneto-optical signals in nonmagnetic semiconductors entangle spin and orbital contributions, both in angular-momentum generation and magneto-optical detection. We calculate these contributions for electron-doped GaAs and Si using density-functional theory, linear-response theory, and a second-order density-matrix treatment of the inverse Faraday effect. At small electron doping, the intrinsic orbital Hall conductivity exceeds its spin counterpart in magnitude, while the orbital contribution to light-induced magnetization dominates over broad photon-energy ranges. We show that orbital- and spin-resolved optical Hall and polar Kerr coefficients exhibit stronger sensitivity to orbital moments than to equal spin moments. This contrast reflects direct electric-dipole coupling to orbital motion versus spin-orbit-mediated coupling to spin polarization. Consequently, Si maintains a substantial orbital magneto-optical response despite its weak spin-orbit interaction. At probe energies of 1.5 eV in GaAs and 3.0 eV in Si, the magnitude of the Kerr rotation per unit orbital moment is approximately 5 and 13 times larger than that per unit spin moment, respectively. Combining the calculated Hall conductivities and Kerr coefficients with a phenomenological drift-diffusion model yields predominantly orbital edge signals for the assumed diffusion constants and relaxation lengths. These results indicate that optical detection of induced magnetization in doped semiconductors such as GaAs and Si can be dominated by orbital signals, and therefore cannot be interpreted solely in terms of spin polarization.

title: Neutron Spin Resonance as Probe of Triplet Pair Density Waves in CeCoIn$_5$
summary: Spin resonance modes are among the most characteristic collective excitations of unconventional superconductors, yet their microscopic origin remains unresolved. Although commonly interpreted as purely magnetic excitations, this picture does not explain the rich magnetic field evolution of these modes observed in heavy-fermion superconductors. Here we combine inelastic neutron scattering and symmetry analysis to investigate the evolution of the spin resonance modes in the heavy-fermion superconductor CeCoIn$_5$ under an in-plane magnetic field. At high fields, approaching the upper critical field of the superconductor, we discover a third resonance mode with relatively high intensity. We demonstrate that the resonance branches observed experimentally can be interpreted as collective modes of the superconducting condensate involving transitions to excited superconducting states. This framework provides a unified interpretation of the field-induced splitting of the resonance, the newly observed mode at high fields, the relative neutron scattering intensities of each mode, and provides the first direct evidence that a spin resonance mode can be associated with a singlet-triplet excitation of a superconductor.

title: Edge-asymmetric magnetism in semi-Dirac quantum dots
summary: In this study, we investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of quantum dots (QDs) throughout the transition from the Dirac limit to the semi-Dirac limit and beyond. When non-interacting semi-Dirac fermions are confined in triangular QDs, the resulting electronic states near the Fermi level are localized asymmetrically among the three edges of these systems. In the presence of electron interactions, we show that these low-energy states favor the formation of edge-asymmetric magnetism in triangular QDs. In particular, the magnetic moments were localized only along a single edge of the zigzag triangular QDs, corresponding to an edge-asymmetric ferromagnetic ground state. For various system sizes, these zigzag triangular QDs exhibit a one-unit increase in the ground-state total spin ($ΔS_z = +1$) beyond the semi-Dirac limit, revealing a striking result of this transition. In contrast, the remaining two edges are antiferromagnetically coupled in the armchair triangular QDs, indicating an edge-asymmetric antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground state. We further identified the AFM ground states in hexagonal QDs, indicating that these types of asymmetric configurations are not unique to triangular QDs. Collectively, edge-asymmetric magnetism could create potential opportunities for future spintronics.

title: Perfect Spin-to-Charge Signal Conversion via Inverse Spin Hall Effect in a Superconductor
summary: Spin-to-charge conversion is central to spintronics, but conventional spin Hall mechanisms are intrinsically limited by the small spin Hall angle. Here we show that superconductivity can overcome this limitation and enable near-unity spin-to-charge signal conversion. We consider a nonlocal spin-valve geometry in which a spin accumulation is injected into a superconductor and converted into a transverse charge signal through the inverse spin Hall effect. In the superconducting state, the strongly suppressed quasiparticle conductance below the gap allows the resulting charge imbalance to generate a voltage comparable to the injected spin bias, despite a small spin Hall angle. We derive the full nonequilibrium response including finite spectral broadening and finite temperature, and propose temperature and spin-bias-dependent measurements of the detector voltage to test our predictions.

title: Scanning nanowire quantum dot with radio-frequency read-out
summary: Scanning single-electron transistors (SETs) are highly sensitive local probes of charge and electric potential, but their integration with robust height control for scanning probe microscopy remains challenging. Furthermore, readout bandwidths are limited to tens of kHz, while characterizing faster charge dynamics is often of interest. Here, we present a scanning SET in the form of a nanowire (NW) quantum dot (QD) integrated at the apex of a non-contact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) cantilever. We demonstrate NC-AFM topographic imaging and local electrometry capability by mapping the electrostatic potential generated by a set of nanoscale voltage-biased gate electrodes. Comparison with electrostatic simulations shows agreement with the measured potential profiles. We demonstrate radio-frequency (rf) reflectometry read-out of the sensor, by embedding the QD in an LC-resonator. This platform establishes a route towards high-bandwidth scanning electrometry with simultaneous topographic contrast.

title: All-in-one Spintronic Sensory Neurons for Magnetic Edge Intelligence
summary: Magnetic fields enable non-contact sensing through nonmagnetic materials, offering opportunities for magnetic edge intelligence in autonomous recognition, navigation, and control. However, directly converting magnetic stimuli into neural spikes for local neuromorphic processing remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate an all-in-one spintronic sensory neuron (SSN) based on spin-transfer-torque magnetic tunnel junctions (STT-MTJs) fabricated using a 40-nm magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) process. By exploiting magnetic-field-modulated stochastic switching, the SSN enables probability-based sensing with an electrically tunable sensitive field window, allowing adaptive operation across different magnetic-field ranges without structural modification. This tunability alleviates the fixed sensitivity-range constraint of conventional tunneling magnetoresistance sensing, providing an accessible sensing range of +/-40 mT with an average probability sensitivity of 2.91%/mT. Importantly, the same stochastic switching process directly transduces magnetic stimuli into binary spike trains, integrating magnetic sensing, nonlinear rate encoding, and spike generation within a single nanoscale device. The resulting sigmoidal spike-rate response enables magnetic-field encoding, experimentally validated using the Neural Engineering Framework. Using experimentally characterized device responses, a simulated 10 x 10 SSN array achieves 90.7% accuracy in contactless magnetic-trajectory recognition with optimized encoding, approaching the software baseline. These results establish a scalable, MRAM-compatible approach to unifying programmable magnetic sensing and neural encoding for sensor-native edge intelligence.

title: Two-dimensional Thyristor
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer a viable platform for next-generation electronics beyond sub-3 nm nodes, yet essential nonlinear circuit elements, such as thyristors, remain unexplored on atomically thin platforms. Here, we report an atomically thin reconfigurable electro-optical thyristor based on a lateral WSe2-MoSe2-WSe2-MoSe2 PNPN heterostructure, directly grown via sequential edge epitaxy. Unlike single-junction 2D diodes, this multijunction architecture exhibits thyristor-like nonlinear switching, including forward blocking, abrupt snapback, bistability, and electrical latching. The device exhibits a forward-blocking voltage of 183 V, corresponding to a critical electric field of 1 MV/cm. Under open-gate conditions, avalanche-assisted carrier multiplication and regenerative feedback are associated with a sharp forward-voltage drop of 175 V, a pronounced current surge, and an ultralow holding voltage. Gate-pulse modulation and temperature-dependent measurements indicate avalanche-assisted thyristor operation and latching behavior. This 2D lateral heterostructure enables a new route to nonlinear and bistable switching, latching, ultralow standby power, and adaptive logic, opening the way for reconfigurable 2D electronics and photonic integrated circuits.

title: Aharonov-Bohm oscillations in transport through interacting quantum dots
summary: We investigate electronic transport through a two-terminal Aharonov-Bohm interferometer with two quantum dots in the presence of finite intra-dot Coulomb interactions. With the help of a diagrammatic technique, we derive, within linear perturbation theory in the tunnelling-coupling strength, analytic expressions for the occupations, current, and interferometric visibility in terms of a coherence measure that involves the sum of four off-diagonal elements of the reduced density matrix. The latter are calculated numerically from a master equation for arbitrary settings of the system parameters. For some symmetric setups, we obtain closed-form expressions for the linear conductance. We systematically analyse the impact of a finite Coulomb interaction on the interferometric visibility, and reveal a rapid suppression of destructive interference upon breaking of system symmetries. Our results are supported by alternative methods, including the TraSPI method.

title: Interaction-driven ordering of multiple pseudospins and anomalous Hall metals in Bernal-stacked graphene
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures + Supplemental Material (4 pages, 1 figure)
summary: Recent observations of anomalous Hall states in Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene raise a fundamental question: How do electron-electron interactions organize multiple low-energy pseudospin sectors within each spin-valley flavor? Within the Hartree-Fock approximation, we analyze interaction-driven pseudospin ordering and spin-valley polarization as functions of displacement field and carrier density. We find a rich phase diagram shaped by the interplay between the two pseudospin doublets, including mixed flavor orders at charge neutrality and anomalous Hall metals upon doping. In particular, we identify topological states with $σ_{xy} \approx 6e^{2}/h$, consistent with recent experimental observations. Our results highlight the central role of multiple pseudospin doublets in the interaction-driven phases of even-layer Bernal multilayers.

title: Molecular Pawns on a Surface Chessboard: Computational Investigation of Nanographenes with Atomistic Methods
summary: Atomically precise nanographenes combine tunable electronic topology with localized, coherent spin states, making them candidate platforms for molecular quantum technologies. This review examines the multiscale theoretical framework governing these systems: the hierarchy of computational methods for describing magnetic properties, the substrate-molecule interface, on-surface synthetic kinetics, and supramolecular self-assembly. We highlight how density functional theory, automated reaction-path discovery, and spin-aware machine-learned interatomic potentials connect static electronic structure to mesoscale dynamics, and how magnetic exchange, optical excitations, and spin transport can be predicted before synthesis.

title: Dirac-like bands and weak-field transverse transport in ABA trilayer graphene
summary: The low-energy electronic structure of ABA trilayer graphene is composed of light and heavy electron branches, which can be altered by an out-of-plane displacement field. Here, we show that, depending on the values of Slonczewski-Weiss-McClure parameters, a displacement field can inflict a band edge inversion, for which we identify the inversion conditions. This inversion is accompanied by a reversal of Berry curvature and giant topological magnetic moments at the band edges. In a weak perpendicular magnetic field, those topological magnetic moments produce valley splitting, giving rise to distinct anomalous transverse electrical and thermoelectric responses. These features offer a potential route to detecting the band inversion and constraining several of the least established tight-binding parameters, such as the on-site energy shift for the dimer pair of carbons $Δ^\prime$ and the next neighbour hopping parameters $γ_2$ and $γ_5$.

title: LeIFF: A localized-electron and ion force field for coupled nuclear and electronic dynamics
comment: Main text: 21 pages (including references), 13 figures, 3 tables; Supplementary Information: 22 pages, 26 figures, 3 tables
summary: Classical and machine-learned interatomic potentials enable large-scale simulations by replacing electronic structure with an effective energy surface for nuclear motion. This excludes electronic dynamics, electronic excitation and energy exchange between electrons and ions. First-principles electron dynamics can describe these processes, but its computational cost restricts system sizes and simulation times. Electron force fields offer an intermediate description by treating electrons as semiclassical dynamical particles interacting with ions. We introduce the localized-electron and ion force field (LeIFF), a compact physical model for both ground state bonding and excited electron dynamics. Valence electrons are represented by spin-labeled spherical charge distributions with dynamical centers and widths. The energy combines analytic electronic kinetic, Coulomb, and dispersion terms with spline-interpolated short-range interactions fitted to a large molecular data set. The resulting energy surface describes a variety of ground state properties across diverse bonding environments and charge states. It also provides a qualitative description of electronic behavior away from equilibrium. It shows improved robustness, accuracy, and transferability relative to earlier electron force-fields. Without any solid-state training, the same model describes dielectric screening and collective electronic response in silicon. LeIFF thus opens a route to large-scale simulations of nonadiabatic processes in molecules and solids, combining chemical bonding and nonequilibrium electronic motion within a common physical framework.

title: Protected Charge Readout Scheme Utilizing Nonlinear Resonators
summary: Charge detection of nanoscale quantum devices commonly relies on dissipative sensors, where signal absorption causes measurement backaction. Recently, nonlinear resonators showed a near-unity readout signal through an induced frequency shift. We show that this frequency shift protects the sensor, as it detunes the resonator from the measurement signal. The resonator excitation reduces while an enhanced readout signal is maintained. Our results, supported by numerical modeling, show that nonlinear resonators can combine strong readout contrast with reduced measurement-induced backaction.

title: Spin-controlled thermophase and noise-optimized thermometry in multiorbital quantum dots
summary: Converting temperature differences into electrical signals underlies both thermoelectric energy conversion and thermometry, which is essential for managing heat in cryogenic quantum technologies. Superconducting circuits typically show a weak thermoelectric response, since their quasiparticle spectrum is nearly particle-hole symmetric. In a Josephson junction, a temperature difference can instead be converted into a superconducting phase difference in an open circuit. We investigate this thermophase effect in a setup where the junction consists of a two-orbital quantum dot with Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Zeeman splitting. A second orbital near the superconducting coherence peaks supports quasiparticle transport over a broad gate range. Zeeman splitting can enhance the thermophase by suppressing pair transport, while spin-orbit hybridization shifts the orbital resonances and can reverse the sign of the response. We assess the junction as a phase-based thermometer using a noise budget that includes readout and current noise together with fluctuations of the orbital energies and the magnetic field. The optimal operating points do not maximize the thermophase but balance a large quasiparticle response against sensitivity to parameter fluctuations. Under experimentally motivated noise assumptions, we obtain projected noise-equivalent temperatures of order $10\,μ\mathrm{K}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and determine the range over which a linear calibration remains accurate. Gate-tunable quantum-dot junctions thus offer a phase-based route to sensing temperature differences in superconducting circuits at sub-kelvin temperatures.
